screens.title: Debugging, Testing, and Deployment of React Native Apps
screens.subtitle: From stepping through code to shipping a signed app to stores

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn to diagnose and fix runtime problems, write reliable unit tests, and prepare a React Native app for iOS and Android distribution. We will use practical tools that are common in professional mobile workflows: the React Native Debugger for breakpoint-driven JavaScript inspection, Flipper for native and network diagnostics, and Jest with React Native Testing Library for tests that assert user-visible behavior. You will also learn the difference between running inside Expo Go and building a standalone app, plus the extra steps needed in bare React Native projects when working with Xcode and Android Studio. Each section includes concrete examples, common mistakes to avoid, and a short hands-on activity you can follow along with. By the end you will understand how to step through an onPress handler, write a simple component test, and package a build that reviewers will accept in app stores. Keep in mind: debugging and testing reduce risk; deployment requires configuration and care. As you progress, ask yourself what failure modes testing will catch and which require runtime inspection.

keyIdea.title: Chapter focus
keyIdea.text: Use the right debugging tools, write user-focused tests, and follow deployment best practices to deliver stable, secure React Native apps.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These first objectives set the groundwork for practical skills you will use immediately. You will learn how to use common debugging tools to step through JavaScript execution and inspect component state. This helps you diagnose complex state issues that simple logs cannot reveal. Next, you will understand the basics of unit testing React Native components using Jest and React Native Testing Library, focusing on tests that assert user-visible behavior rather than internal implementation. Writing such tests gives you confidence to refactor and evolve your UI safely. Each objective pairs theory with hands-on examples so you can practice setting breakpoints, running tests, and interpreting results. As you move through the lesson, consider which bugs are best solved with a debugger and which should have been prevented by a test. That contrast will guide where to invest your time when building robust apps.

screens.title: Why use a debugger in React Native?
screens.subtitle: Breakpoints, stepping, and inspecting component state

narration.text: A debugger gives you a precise way to observe what your app is doing at runtime. Instead of inferring behavior from printed logs, a debugger lets you pause execution, inspect variables, and step line-by-line through JavaScript code. In React Native, using the React Native Debugger or Flipper means you can set breakpoints inside event handlers, watch the value of props and state, and evaluate expressions in the current context. For example, when an onPress handler updates state incorrectly, setting a breakpoint at the start of the handler lets you see whether the function receives the expected values and whether setState calls are using the right value or the functional updater. A common misconception is that console. log is always sufficient. Console logs are helpful for quick checks but can be misleading in asynchronous or timing-sensitive code. Remote debugging connects your JS runtime to desktop developer tools, letting you step through the exact execution path while you reproduce the bug. As a practical exercise, enable remote debugging, set a breakpoint in a small counter component, trigger the action, and step through the handler to observe the variable lifecycle. The takeaway: use a debugger for timing, closure, and complex state problems that logs cannot reliably reveal. Which state transitions in your app would benefit most from a breakpoint-based inspection?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A debugger pauses execution so you can inspect runtime values, step through code, and resolve timing or closure issues that logs can't expose.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Why use a debugger?
Core Concept
Why use a debugger in React Native?
Breakpoints, stepping, and inspecting component state
A debugger gives you precise visibility into execution flow. When you set a breakpoint you freeze the runtime and can inspect call stacks, variables, and closures. This is essential for diagnosing timing issues and stale closures that lead to unexpected state updates. Use the debugger when the problem depends on order of operations, asynchronous callbacks, or complex interactions between components.
Example
Pause an onPress handler that updates state and step through to see whether the functional updater is used or a stale value is read.
Common mistake
Relying only on console.log for timing-sensitive bugs can hide race conditions.
Debugger Walkthrough
Enable Remote JS
Open dev menu and choose Debug Remote JS; then use developer tools to set breakpoints.
Inspect Variables
Watch props, state, and closures to see how values change during execution.
Step & Evaluate
Step into functions and evaluate expressions to test hypotheses.
Practical Tip
Set breakpoints near state setters to confirm the update pattern and avoid stale closures.
Key Takeaway

Use a debugger to examine execution order and state transitions; reserve console logs for quick checks but rely on breakpoints for complex timing issues.

screens.title: React Native Debugger: how to step through code
screens.subtitle: Opening the debugger, setting breakpoints, and inspecting execution

narration.text: React Native Debugger combines the familiar Chrome DevTools with React Developer Tools and Redux DevTools into a single workflow for JavaScript debugging. To use it, run your app and open the developer menu — on simulators this is Cmd+D for iOS or Cmd+M for Android, or shake a real device — then enable remote debugging. This connects the app's JavaScript VM to the desktop tools so you can set breakpoints and step through code. A concrete example: place a breakpoint inside an increment handler of a counter component, then trigger the event. When execution pauses, inspect the component's state and the event object to confirm inputs are as expected. One common misconception is that remote debugging changes the app's timing; it can, so use it alongside device logs and device-based tools when diagnosing subtle race conditions. Remember to disable remote debugging for performance measurements since the JS runs in a different process when remote-debugging. Finally, use the React tab to inspect component hierarchies and props; that view helps you correlate a paused stack frame to the UI you see on screen. After stepping through, reflect on which closure or order-of-operations issues the debugger revealed and how a small unit test could prevent the same bug in the future.

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Open remote debugging, set breakpoints, step through execution, and inspect component state and props to diagnose runtime behavior.

Key Takeaway

Use step debugging to confirm the exact sequence of operations and protect against subtle closure and timing bugs that logs cannot reliably expose.

screens.title: Flipper and the developer ecosystem
screens.subtitle: Inspecting network, databases, and native state

narration.text: Flipper is a platform for debugging mobile apps that provides native plugins to inspect networking, databases, and layout information across iOS, Android, and React Native. Unlike a pure JavaScript debugger, Flipper can attach to native layers so you can view network requests, inspect SQLite or async storage data, and see the native view hierarchy. For bare React Native projects this is especially valuable, because native issues often involve bridging or module configuration. A concrete scenario: you suspect an A P I call is failing silently. Flipper's network plugin shows the request and response payload so you can verify headers and server errors. Another common misconception is assuming that JavaScript-only tools are sufficient; if your bug involves native modules or configuration, only a native-aware tool like Flipper will reveal the problem. Use Flipper in conjunction with the React Native Debugger: use Flipper for native inspection and RN Debugger for stepping through JS logic. The practical benefit is faster triage when bugs cross the JS/native boundary. Reflect on which bugs in your project might require native plugins to inspect and what telemetry you should enable for production monitoring.

keyIdea.title: Flipper
keyIdea.text: An extensible platform that inspects native and JS layers: network, DBs, layout, and plugins for deeper diagnostics.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Flipper
Definition
Flipper and the developer ecosystem
Inspect network requests, databases, and the native view hierarchy.
Flipper connects to both native and JavaScript layers, making it well-suited to diagnose issues that cross boundaries. For instance, a misconfigured native module that fails to initialize will appear in the native logs and may show missing data in database viewers. When you suspect a failing API call, the network inspector reveals request headers, payload, and server response so you don't guess at what the server returned. Because Flipper offers plugins, you can add debuggers for custom tooling or databases used in your app. Combine Flipper with JS debugging to correlate native events with JavaScript behavior.
Network
Inspect requests, headers, and responses.
Database
View SQLite, Realm, or AsyncStorage contents.
Layout
Inspect native view hierarchies for rendering issues.
Supporting Explanation
  • Flipper is especially useful in bare projects where native configuration matters.
  • Use the network panel to confirm server errors or incorrect headers instead of guessing from UI failures.
  • Inspect local databases to find corrupted or unexpected stored data that affects app logic.
Concrete Scenario
You notice a list missing items. Flipper shows that data fetched from the server returned a malformed JSON response, revealing the true source of the issue.
Key Takeaway

Use Flipper to inspect native and network layers; it complements JS debuggers when issues cross the native/JS boundary.

screens.title: Expo Developer Tools and Expo Go
screens.subtitle: When Expo simplifies debugging and when it restricts you

narration.text: Expo offers a managed workflow that speeds development by handling native build complexity for you. During development, you typically run your app in Expo Go — a universal client that downloads and runs your JavaScript bundle. This provides rapid iteration without rebuilding native binaries. The benefit is simplicity: Expo Developer Tools and the Expo CLI give you logs, network inspection, and an easy path to publish or build an app. The trade-off is that Expo Go cannot include arbitrary custom native modules; if your app depends on a native library not included in Expo Go, you must create a standalone build or eject to the bare workflow. A common misconception is that Expo removes all native work for production; in reality, creating a standalone app requires a build step that bundles your JavaScript and any native dependencies. For a concrete example: testing a new native camera plugin will fail inside Expo Go, but succeed after a standalone build that includes the native module. Use Expo Go for fast prototyping and standalone builds or the bare workflow for maximum flexibility. Before committing to Expo for a project, audit required native modules to ensure they are supported or plan a migration path.

keyIdea.title: Expo Go vs Standalone
keyIdea.text: Expo Go enables fast development but lacks custom native modules; standalone builds include all native dependencies and are required for app store submission when native code is used.

screens.title: Testing strategy: unit, integration, and E2E
screens.subtitle: What each test level guarantees and when to use it

narration.text: Testing in React Native typically falls into three layers: unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests. Unit tests validate the smallest pieces—functions and small components—often mocking external dependencies to keep tests focused and fast. Integration tests exercise a component together with nearby collaborators to ensure they interact correctly. End-to-end tests drive the whole app like a real user, validating critical flows from launch to completion. A common testing mistake is writing tests tightly coupled to implementation details; instead, prefer assertions on the visible UI and user interactions. React Native Testing Library encourages this user-centric approach by exposing queries for text and accessibility labels rather than component internals. A concrete example: test that a button press increments a visible counter rather than checking internal state variables. Use unit tests for pure logic, integration tests for component interactions, and E2E tests for critical user journeys like login or purchases. Each layer has trade-offs: unit tests are fast but may miss integration bugs; E2E tests catch regressions but are slower and more brittle. Compose a test pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a handful of well-chosen E2E tests for core flows. Which user flows in your app deserve an E2E check before release?

keyIdea.title: Testing Pyramid
keyIdea.text: Use unit tests for logic, integration tests for interactions, and E2E tests for critical user journeys; prefer user-focused assertions.

content.html:

Testing strategy: unit, integration, and E2E
Choose the right test level for each concern and prefer user-focused assertions.
Unit Tests
Fast, isolated tests for functions or components.

E2E Tests

Concrete Example
Test a counter by asserting the displayed text increments when the button is pressed, not by examining internal state. This keeps tests resilient to implementation changes.
Misconception

Testing implementation details leads to brittle tests; prefer user-observable outcomes instead.

screens.title: Jest and React Native Testing Library
screens.subtitle: Tools that help test components from the user's perspective

narration.text: Jest is the standard testing framework for JavaScript and React Native; it provides test running, assertions, mocking, and snapshot testing. When paired with React Native Testing Library, you write tests that focus on how users interact with your UI. React Native Testing Library exposes queries like getByText to find visible elements and fireEvent to simulate interactions. A concrete code example from the chapter demonstrates testing a MyButton component: render the component with a title, then assert the text appears and that the mock onPress function is called when the button is pressed. A common mistake is mocking too much or testing internal state rather than the rendered result. Instead, mock external services and assert the visible UI. Running tests with npm test runs Jest and reports passed and failed cases. Use descriptive test names and keep tests small and focused. When a test fails, decide whether the failure indicates a bug or a brittle test tied to implementation; if the latter, refactor the test to reflect user behavior. Good tests act as documentation and enable safe refactoring. What user-visible behavior in your app would benefit most from a focused Jest test?

keyIdea.title: Jest + Testing Library
keyIdea.text: Use Jest to run tests and React Native Testing Library to assert user-visible component behavior and interactions.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Jest & Testing Library
Definition
Jest and React Native Testing Library
Write tests that assert what users see and do.
Jest runs and reports tests, while React Native Testing Library gives you queries that reflect the UI. This combination encourages tests that focus on the user's experience rather than internal implementation. Use mock functions for callbacks and assert on rendered text or accessibility labels when possible.
Code Example
// __tests__/MyButton.test.js
import React from 'react';
import { render, fireEvent } from '@testing-library/react-native';
import MyButton from '../components/MyButton';

describe('MyButton', () => {
  it('renders correctly with given title', () => {
    const { getByText } = render();
    expect(getByText('Press Me')).toBeTruthy();
  });

  it('calls onPress when button is pressed', () => {
    const mockOnPress = jest.fn();
    const { getByText } = render();

    fireEvent.press(getByText('Test Button'));

    expect(mockOnPress).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  });
});
Key Takeaway

Write tests that mirror user interactions: render, find, interact, then assert visible outcome to keep tests resilient and useful.

screens.title: Write a basic unit test: Greeting component
screens.subtitle: Render a component and assert visible text

narration.text: Let's walk through a minimal unit test that focuses on rendered output. The Greeting component takes a name prop and displays a friendly message. In the test, render the component with a concrete name and assert that the greeting text appears. This approach verifies the component's contract from the user's perspective. A common mistake is asserting internal state or implementation-specific class names; instead, use getByText or accessibility queries. Running the test with npm test will execute the Jest runner and report whether the rendered text matches expectations. If the test fails, ask whether the component's visible contract changed intentionally or if the code regressed. If intentional, update the test; if not, fix the component. This simple pattern scales: small, focused tests for each component reduce the cognitive load when debugging a failing integration or E2E flow. After writing the test, reflect on how it would have caught a future regression and what other UI elements deserve the same protection. Write a basic unit test: Greeting component means render the component and assert visible text rather than checking internal implementation.. In practical terms, render a component and assert visible text. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Example Test
keyIdea.text: Render the component and assert visible text rather than checking internal implementation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Greeting Test
Hands-on Activity
Write a basic unit test: Greeting component
Render and assert visible text to verify the user-facing contract.
This small test shows how to keep unit tests focused and resilient. It demonstrates rendering the component, querying for the expected text, and asserting presence. Use this pattern for small presentational components and avoid reaching into internals to keep maintenance costs low.
Code Example
// components/Greeting.js
import React from 'react';
import { Text, View } from 'react-native';

export default function Greeting({ name }) {
  return (
    <View>
      <Text>Hello, {name}!</Text>
    </View>
  );
}

// __tests__/Greeting.test.js
import React from 'react';
import { render } from '@testing-library/react-native';
import Greeting from '../components/Greeting';

describe('Greeting', () => {
  it('renders the correct greeting message', () => {
    const { getByText } = render(<Greeting name="Cohortia" />);
    expect(getByText('Hello, Cohortia!')).toBeTruthy();
  });
});
Key Takeaway

Small, user-focused tests make refactoring safer and reduce the likelihood of shipping regressions that affect visible behavior.

screens.title: Running tests and common pitfalls
screens.subtitle: npm test, jest config, and avoiding brittle tests

narration.text: Running your test suite is straightforward: use npm test to invoke Jest. Ensure your project has the necessary dev dependencies, including @testing-library/react-native and react-test-renderer, and a Jest configuration appropriate for React Native. When writing tests, prefer queries that reflect user intent — getByText or getByRole — and avoid assertions on implementation specifics. Common pitfalls include mocking too much, which can hide integration issues, or writing tests that depend on component internals that change frequently. Another issue is flaky tests caused by asynchronous operations; be explicit about awaits and use findBy queries or waitFor to handle eventual updates. For code that accesses native modules, mock them consistently in test setup to avoid runtime errors in the Node environment. When a test fails, triage whether the failure indicates a behavioral regression or a brittle test tied to a refactor; fix the code if it regressed, or update the test to assert observable behavior. Regularly run tests locally and in CI to catch platform-specific issues early. Consider adding a small set of E2E checks for critical flows if you notice regressions that unit tests miss. Which tests in your suite are most likely to prevent shipping a regression?

keyIdea.title: Test Hygiene
keyIdea.text: Run tests with npm test, mock native modules, wait for async updates, and prefer user-centric assertions to avoid brittle tests.

content.html:

screens.title: Deployment with Expo
screens.subtitle: Building standalone apps and the simplified Expo workflow

narration.text: Expo simplifies the build process by handling many native steps for you. Using the Expo CLI you can request builds for iOS and Android, and Expo will produce an. ipa for iOS or an. apk/. aab for Android. With Expo Application Services you can run managed builds in the cloud, which takes care of signing and provisioning when configured. The process is straightforward: audit native modules to ensure compatibility with Expo, run the build command, and then download the resulting artifacts for store submission. A common misconception is that Expo always handles signing automatically; you still need to provide credentials or use service-managed credentials. For production, test the standalone build on real devices to confirm native behaviors and permissions work as expected. After creating the package, follow platform-specific store guidelines and verify that privacy and permission disclosures are correct. The concrete benefit of Expo is reduced build complexity for many projects, allowing teams to focus on JavaScript code, but remember to plan for a standalone build step when you approach release milestones. Deployment with Expo means use expo cli or eas to create standalone app packages; expo reduces build complexity but requires credential management for production signing.. In practical terms, building standalone apps and the simplified expo workflow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Expo Builds
keyIdea.text: Use Expo CLI or EAS to create standalone app packages; Expo reduces build complexity but requires credential management for production signing.

screens.title: Bare React Native builds, signing, and release checklist
screens.subtitle: Xcode, Gradle, certificates, and pre-release checks

narration.text: When you work in a bare React Native project you gain full native control but also take on the responsibility of configuring Xcode and Android Studio for builds. For iOS, prepare provisioning profiles and signing certificates in the Apple Developer portal and configure them in Xcode. For Android, configure Gradle signing in your build. gradle and generate a keystore. These steps are required to produce archives suitable for App Store or Play Store submission. A common mistake is shipping builds with debug settings or leaving A P I keys in code. Before release, profile performance to find slow rendering or heavy re-renders, use FlatList for long lists, and optimize images. Secure sensitive keys by moving them to environment variables or secure storage solutions and never hardcode them. Test on multiple devices and screen sizes, verify permissions and privacy messages, and prepare analytics and crash reporting to monitor production. The release checklist should include building a signed artifact, testing it on devices, confirming analytics and privacy disclosures, and ensuring crash reporting is enabled. This reduces risk during app review and gives you production visibility once users install your app.

keyIdea.title: Release Checklist
keyIdea.text: Configure signing, optimize performance, secure secrets, test on devices, and enable analytics/crash reporting before submission.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Bare Builds & Checklist

Bare React Native builds, signing, and release checklist
Prepare Xcode and Gradle, secure keys, and verify performance.
For iOS, configure provisioning profiles and certificates; for Android, generate a keystore and configure Gradle signing. Avoid shipping debug builds or embedding secrets directly in source. Use secure storage for keys and environment variables for build-time secrets. Profile for re-render hotspots and optimize lists and large images. Enable analytics and crash reporting before release to gather production feedback and prioritize fixes after launch.
Pre-release Checklist
Signing
Configure certificates/profiles for iOS and keystore/Gradle for Android.
Performance
Use FlatList, lazy load images, and minimize unnecessary re-renders.
Security & Privacy

Key Takeaway

A careful release checklist reduces app review friction and ensures you can monitor and respond to production issues effectively.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Debugging & Testing
screens.subtitle: Compact reminders of tools and testing philosophy

narration.text: Remember these core concepts as you debug and test React Native apps. First, React Native Debugger gives you breakpoint-based inspection that is essential for timing and closure issues. Second, Flipper provides native-level inspection for network, database, and view hierarchy problems that cross the JS/native boundary. Third, Jest and React Native Testing Library encourage tests that emulate user interactions and confirm visible behavior rather than internal implementation. Together, these tools make a development workflow where you can reproduce issues, write tests that prevent regressions, and triage complex bugs faster. A useful habit is to write a small test for critical components and, when an elusive bug appears, use the debugger or Flipper to trace it. This combination reduces debugging time and increases confidence in releases. Which of these tools will you adopt first in your workflow, and for which class of problems?

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Use debuggers for runtime inspection, Flipper for native issues, and tests that assert user-visible behavior.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Deployment & Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Essentials for shipping stable, secure apps

narration.text: Before you ship, remember the practical essentials that protect users and reduce review friction. First, know the difference between Expo Go and a standalone build: use Expo Go for development but produce a standalone package for app stores. Second, follow release best practices: sign builds correctly, optimize performance using FlatList and image optimizations, and secure secrets using environment variables or secure storage. Third, test on real devices, prepare privacy disclosures, and enable analytics and crash reporting to monitor production. These practices prevent common submission issues and give you the telemetry to respond to problems after release. When faced with a last-minute decision, prioritize security and platform requirements over convenience; an unsigned or misconfigured build can delay publication. Which release checklist item will you add to your next build pipeline to reduce risk?

keyIdea.title: Deployment Essentials
keyIdea.text: Produce signed standalone builds, optimize and secure your app, test on devices, and enable production monitoring.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Deployment Essentials
Key Concepts — Deployment & Best Practices
Three focused reminders before release
Expo vs Standalone
Use Expo Go for development; create standalone builds for stores and native modules.
Performance
Optimize lists, images, and rendering to ensure responsive UX across devices.
Security & Privacy
Remove hardcoded keys, use secure storage, and prepare privacy disclosures for stores.
Final Summary

A careful release process combines correct builds, performance optimization, and security practices with pre-release testing to create a smooth app store submission and reliable production experience.

Create a 15-minute mixed-format lesson. Start with a screen recording demonstrating the React Native Debugger: show how to enable remote debugging, set a breakpoint in a simple component's `onPress` handler, and step through the code, inspecting variables. Then, transition to a slide deck for 3 minutes explaining Jest and React Native Testing Library's philosophy. Follow with a live coding demo for 5 minutes: create a new simple component (e.g., a `Header` with a title) and write a basic unit test for it using `@testing-library/react-native`, showing `render` and `getByText`. Finally, dedicate 2 minutes to a visual explanation (diagrams) of the Expo build process for iOS and Android, contrasting Expo Go with standalone builds. Include a reflection prompt on the importance of testing.
